description: We’re MCP Mission Control, building at the intersection of space storytelling, live community engagement, and AI agents. For NASA’s “Abandoned but not Forgotten,” we’re creating a Mission Hub that turns discarded Moon/Mars hardware into living, interactive stories via an MCP server consumable by web and AI/MCP clients. Users can explore AI-narrated artifacts, ask real-time questions, join moderated discussions, and view live data cards. Join us to build a real, shippable product.
summary:
Children hear about the rovers driving on Mars today. They rarely hear about the ones that went quiet. Mission Memory turns 17 pieces of NASA hardware resting on the Moon, on Mars and beyond into stories that 9 to 14-year-olds can listen to, play with and keep.

Children turn a radio dial to scan each world. The static clears as the needle reaches an explorer, which sits on a 3D globe at its real NASA coordinates. Then the explorer starts telling its own story. Nine explorers tell full five-chapter stories, each narrated, illustrated with NASA images and cited line by line to NASA sources. Three stories include a hands-on moment: timing a laser to the Moon, driving Spirit with a broken wheel, and holding down Dawn's ion engine. Every story ends with a postcard children can print or share.

The same stories open inside AI assistants as interactive cards, useful for classroom teachers. Every fact comes from NASA's NSSDCA catalog and mission pages, and the team checked every chapter before it went live.
details:
What It Does

1. Tune In: find the explorers

  • Three worlds:
    • The Moon (4 explorers)
    • Mars (8)
    • Beyond (5): asteroids, Ceres, and probes leaving the solar system
    • On the Moon and Mars, each one sits at its NSSDCA landing longitude on a 3D globe wrapped in NASA imagery.
    • In Beyond, each one sits at its launch year on a map of the solar system.
    • Its photo, its status and its first line of story appear, and the narrator reads the line aloud.
    • Its status is part of the story. The Apollo retroreflectors are still reflecting lasers fired from Earth. Spirit's last signal came on 22 March 2010.
  • Mission Log: collects a stamp for every explorer found and every story heard.

2. Stories told by the explorers themselves

Nine explorers, three per world, tell their story in five chapters:

  1. Why I was sent
  2. How I worked
  3. What I discovered
  4. My last day
  5. Where I rest now
  • Two depths:
    • Story reads at a Flesch-Kincaid grade of 4.9.
    • More detail reads at grade 8.6, for older or more curious children.
  • Narration: every chapter is narrated, and Play story tells the whole story by itself.
  • On screen: the text types out as it's read, at the narrator's pace.
  • Pictures: each chapter shows a NASA photograph or illustration. Illustrations are labelled.
  • Sources: under What NASA says, children can see the exact NASA sentences each chapter was built from, with links.

Every explorer without a full story still has its NASA record, its status, and NASA's own summary, narrated.

3. Hands-on moments

Each of these lets children feel the engineering that led to a discovery. A narrator guides them through it.

Fire the laser (Apollo retroreflectors)

Send light to the Moon and stop the clock when it comes back, in about 2.5 seconds. That time gives the distance to the Moon, which is how scientists still measure it today.

Physics: 2 × 384,400 km ÷ 299,792 km/s = 2.56 s

Drive with a broken wheel (Spirit)

One of Spirit's six wheels stopped working, so its team had it drag the broken wheel along. The trench it scraped open exposed soil that was about 90% pure silica, a sign of ancient hot springs or steam vents.

Story facts from NASA's Spirit mission pages

Hold to thrust (Dawn)

Dawn's ion engine pushed with the weight of two sheets of paper. Hold the button to watch that push add up from car speed to faster than sound.

Physics: 0.092 N ÷ 1,217.7 kg (NSSDCA 2007-043A) gives about 23.5 km/h of extra speed per day of thrust

4. A postcard to keep

Every story ends with a postcard from the explorer to the child. Children can print it, download it as an image or share it, and a QR code opens the postcard on any phone.

5. Inside AI assistants

Mission Memory is also an MCP server. When a child or teacher asks an assistant such as Claude to "show me the explorers on Mars", the assistant opens the same tuner, globe, stories and hands-on moments as an interactive card in the chat. The card uses the same reviewed data as the website.

How NASA data powers every explorer

NSSDCA is the backbone. For each explorer, the NSSDCA catalog record supplies its identity, landing coordinates, launch date and final status. NASA mission pages (science.nasa.gov) supply the discoveries, and the NASA Image and Video Library supplies the pictures.

How the data flows:

  1. Scripts pull the NSSDCA records and mission pages, and store every fact with the exact sentence it came from.
  2. Stories are drafted only from those quoted facts.
  3. The team fact-checks and approves every chapter.
  4. At every build, each quote is checked again against the saved text of its NASA page. A quote that doesn't match stops the build.
  5. Approved text is narrated, and the website and the MCP server both read the same files.

Everything is built ahead of time, so the live site makes no NASA calls and keeps working without them.

Evidence it works

Why it matters

  • History children rarely hear: abandoned hardware is where the history happened, and most children only ever hear about missions that are still running.
  • Status as story: "still answering" or "last signal received" makes children ask what happened, and why.
  • Science they can feel: each hands-on moment links one piece of engineering to the science it made possible.
  • Trust: every sentence can be traced back to NASA, so teachers can use it without checking it first.

In a classroom (one lesson):

  1. Tune in together on the board.
  2. Pairs each choose an explorer and listen to its story at the depth that suits them.
  3. Each pair presents the explorer's discovery and its "last day".
  4. Everyone prints a postcard.

Older students can open What NASA says and compare the story with the original NASA sentences.

Tools and technologies

  • Website: React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js (react-three-fiber), with Web Audio for the sound effects
  • Data pipeline: Python scripts that ingest NSSDCA and NASA pages, verify quotes and measure reading level
  • Narration: Kokoro-82M text-to-speech, run locally
  • AI assistants: a Node.js MCP server with MCP Apps interactive cards
  • Hosting: Docker and nginx

Try It: https://missionmemory.kenaff.com/

Source Code (Open Source): https://github.com/iyinusa/mission-memory
